papers.title: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
papers.tldr: Massive activations put up to 99.9% of activation variance on one principal component, which makes SAE features unstable across runs and inflates variance-explained scores. Training the SAE with that component removed and adding it back raises top-50 feature sharing between runs to 73-99.5% and cuts model degradation by up to 44%.
summary: SAEs are usually judged by variance explained and by how much splicing them in damages the model. In many LLMs a few huge activation values dominate the residual stream, and it was unclear how this distorts both metrics and the features people end up studying.

The authors show that massive activations concentrate almost all variance on the first principal component (PC1), which has no unique sparse decomposition, so each SAE run rebuilds it from different features. They measure feature agreement between independent runs and how much non-PC1 variance is left unexplained. Their fix trains the SAE on activations with PC1 projected out and then adds PC1 back to the reconstruction.

In affected models, 47 of the 50 most important features are on average unmatched in a second run (versus about 27 for a random 50), and one dictionary reports 99.96% variance explained while missing 33% of the variance outside PC1. With PC1 removed, top-50 feature sharing rises from 4-39.5% to 73-99.5%, model degradation drops by up to 44% at the same TopK sparsity, and content reconstruction error falls by up to 33.9%. Takeaway: before trusting SAE feature rankings or variance-explained numbers, check how much variance sits on PC1 and consider the projection fix; code and trained SAEs are released. Caveat: gains are given as ranges or "up to" figures and apply to models with massive activations.

papers.title: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific
papers.tldr: A linear map between two models' residual streams, fit only on unlabeled prompts, carries refusal steering directions and probes across 110 model pairs. When the map's prompts cover the tool's operating region, it recovers 102% of the target's own refusal steering and 88-98% of its correctness gain.
summary: Steering vectors and probes are normally found separately inside each model with labeled data, which is costly and makes results hard to reuse. It was unclear whether such tools could be transferred between models, and earlier reports suggested cross-model maps fail across domains.

The authors fit a linear map between residual streams of two models using unlabeled prompts only, then transfer a refusal direction (tested causally by addition and ablation), a correctness direction and a sentiment probe. They cover 110 model pairs from five families, 1B to 72B parameters, including base-to-instruct pairs, with specificity controls and five seeds. They also prove when a linear map should work and derive a label-free coverage score.

A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54% of the target's own refusal steering and 16-77% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises this to 102% and 88-98%, while control directions recover at most 1%. The coverage score tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs. Takeaway: steering directions found in one model can be ported to another for the cost of a few unlabeled in-domain prompts, and the coverage score tells you in advance whether the transfer will work. Caveat: results are for linear maps and the tools tested (refusal, correctness, sentiment); code availability is not stated.

papers.title: Improving Confidence Estimation in Language Models with Linear Representations of Ambiguity
papers.tldr: Difference-in-means directions for input ambiguity exist in LM activations and weakly steer ambiguity judgments. Restricting fine-tuning updates to that subspace (DART) greatly improves calibration without hurting accuracy.
summary: LM confidence scores are poor predictors of whether an answer is right, partly because models do not flag inputs that are inherently ambiguous. If models internally represent ambiguity, those representations could be used to fix calibration.

Using minimal pairs of ambiguous and unambiguous sentences, the authors extract ambiguity directions with difference-in-means and test them by steering. They then propose DART, a fine-tuning method that pushes parameter updates to act within the span of these directions and penalizes activation changes outside that subspace. Evaluation covers multiple-choice and generative QA.

Steering with the ambiguity directions changes the model's ambiguity judgments selectively but only weakly, by the authors' own account. DART greatly improves calibration while keeping accuracy, though the abstract gives no specific numbers or model sizes. Takeaway: a concept direction that is a weak steering lever can still be a strong regularizer when used to constrain fine-tuning, which is a useful pattern for anyone working on steering geometry. Caveat: check the paper for which models and how large the calibration gains are.

papers.title: Linear Probes to Bayesian Manifolds: Geometry of Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, under review at ICLR 2027 (preprint)
papers.tldr: Splits a probe result into four separate claims (decodable, has a shape, the shape belongs to that concept, the model uses it) and tests each with a Bayesian pipeline on arithmetic in three 6-8B LLMs. Most concepts are decodable, but 81% of the shapes found are inherited from related concepts rather than owned.
summary: Linear probes often reveal helices or circles in LLM activations, and these are taken as evidence the model computes with them. Probe accuracy alone mixes several claims, so such conclusions can overreach.

The authors separate decodability, shape, ownership and causal use, and test each with a four-stage Bayesian pipeline. Shapes are selected only when evidence passes a preset threshold, ownership is tested by removing related concepts fixed in advance, and causal use by intervening on the shape. They apply this to two-digit addition and multiplication in GPT-J 6B, Llama 3.1 8B and Pythia 6.9B.

Nearly every concept is decodable, but decoded directions overlap strongly across concepts, and every strongly supported shape is a ribbon (a helix with changing radius) or a torus. Of 1,330 cells with an ownership verdict, 19% of shapes are owned and 81% inherited, yet both move the output about equally often. Intervening on the shape keeps about 61% of the full probe's effect with at most five dimensions versus a median of nine. Takeaway: when you claim a geometric structure in activations, report all four verdicts and control for related concepts, not just probe accuracy. Caveat: limited to arithmetic and three models of similar size.

papers.title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module
papers.tldr: Over 144,000 linear-probing runs on vision and language foundation models show that picking the layer and the module inside it (attention, MLP, norm) jointly beats choosing depth alone. Simple fixed rules recover 42% (vision) and 86% (language) of the best possible gain.
summary: Probing the final layer of a foundation model is often suboptimal, and recent work moved to intermediate layers. But representations are still studied block by block, ignoring the different modules inside each transformer block.

The authors run more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations over vision foundation models and LLMs, probing each module output at each layer instead of only the residual stream. From this they derive fixed strategies: the final-layer feed-forward activation for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth for language.

The best layer-module pair gives much larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed, and module quality varies across layers. The fixed rules beat the standard baseline in most evaluations and recover on average 42% (vision) and 86% (language) of the best-pair gain, with vision gains growing as transfer to downstream data gets harder. Takeaway: when probing or extracting features (for example from an ultrasound or vision backbone), sweep modules as well as layers, or start from the suggested defaults. Caveat: the abstract does not name the exact models or tasks.

papers.title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
papers.tldr: A benchmark of 56 datasets and 46 methods tests whether one tabular model can do generation, imputation and prediction together. Frozen tabular foundation models are strong at prediction and numeric imputation, but faithful joint sampling still favors specialist models.
summary: Tabular generation, imputation and prediction all query the same data distribution but are benchmarked separately. So it is unclear what capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one generalist model can handle all three.

The One Table Benchmark covers 56 datasets, 46 registered methods and 20 capability axes with aligned splits and explicit task definitions. Beyond rank comparisons, the authors train five backbones under all seven non-empty combinations of the three objectives on five datasets with three seeds, and compare fixed generalist models with portfolios of specialists.

Imputation and prediction are linked through numeric recovery and dependence preservation, and generation through predictive utility, while distributional fidelity ranks models differently. Adding a task's own objective gives the largest gains, generation gives the broadest auxiliary benefits, and objective benefits do not simply add. Some generalists beat specialist portfolios on utility but not on fidelity, and frozen foundation models are strong at prediction and numeric imputation. Takeaway: if you use a tabular FM for imputation or synthetic data, check fidelity separately from downstream utility, since the two disagree. Caveat: the abstract reports trends rather than headline numbers.

papers.title: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
papers.tldr: Defines fundamental representational units in networks by fidelity and stability, and proves threshold-activated SAEs can recover them under stated conditions. More stable units turn out to be more monosemantic and compose across layers into human-like concept structure.
summary: Interpreting networks needs a clear notion of what the basic units of a representation are and how they relate to human concepts. SAE features are widely used for this, but there is no agreed definition of a 'true' unit or a criterion for when an SAE has found one.

The paper formally defines fundamental representational units (FRUs) and two criteria for judging them, fidelity and stability. It proves that threshold-activated sparse autoencoders (TSAEs) identify FRUs with high fidelity and stability under certain conditions and checks this with large-scale experiments, then studies how stability relates to monosemanticity and cross-layer composition.

The abstract reports that more stable FRUs are more monosemantic and can be composed across layers to recover semantic organization matching human conceptual structure, but it gives no numbers, models or datasets. Takeaway: run-to-run stability is a useful, cheap filter for picking SAE features worth interpreting, and the threshold-activation variant is the one with theoretical backing here. Caveat: the guarantees hold only 'under appropriate conditions', and without numbers in the abstract the strength of the empirical support is unclear.

papers.title: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
papers.tldr: Splits visual chain-of-thought into separate grounding and reasoning steering vectors, aligns them to another vision-language model's activation space and applies each at its own stage. This transfers 'thinking with images' training-free and beats the best transfer baseline by 1.86 points on average.
summary: Visual chain-of-thought lets vision-language models find and use key image regions while reasoning, but it needs costly post-training tied to one backbone. Existing transfer methods treat it as one capability, which mixes grounding with reasoning and intervenes at the wrong stages.

Viscot-steer extracts separate grounding and reasoning vectors from the layers of a source model associated with each capability. It aligns these vectors with the target model's activation space and steers the grounding layers during bounding-box prediction and the reasoning layers during reasoning-trace generation, without any training.

Across high-resolution understanding, general perception and reasoning, and visual math benchmarks, the method transfers capabilities from several visual-CoT models to architecturally different targets and beats the strongest transfer baseline by 1.86 points on average. Takeaway: decomposing a capability into stage-specific vectors and applying each only where it acts is a reusable recipe for cross-model steering. Caveat: the average gain is modest and the abstract does not list the target models or variance across runs.

papers.title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, extended abstract at NeurReps workshop, NeurIPS 2026
papers.tldr: Derives a scalar from attention weights alone that measures how strongly a head can couple to rotary position encodings. It predicts induction heads with Spearman correlation of -0.55 to -0.74 across four RoPE models from 135M to 7B, with no forward passes.
summary: Finding specialized heads such as induction heads usually needs forward passes over data. A data-free way to characterize heads from weights would make analysis of large models cheaper.

The author derives rho, an invariant built from the symmetries of attention that measures a head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings (RoPE), computed from weights only. It is tested on four bias-free RoPE models spanning 135M to 7B parameters, and used as a proof of concept to apply YaRN context extension only to the top-50% positional heads.

Rho predicts induction heads with Spearman correlation between -0.55 and -0.74 across the four models, and applying YaRN only to high-rho heads hurts perplexity less than applying it uniformly. Takeaway: weight-only head statistics can pre-screen heads before running circuit analysis, which saves compute on big models. Caveat: this is a short workshop extended abstract, the YaRN result is described as preliminary, and it applies only to bias-free RoPE models; code is released.

papers.title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models
papers.tldr: Uses a pretrained tabular foundation model as a training-free dynamics model by treating next-state prediction as in-context regression. It beats LSTMs and MLPs trained on the same scarce data, but rollouts degrade with short context and inference is about 1000 times slower than an LSTM.
summary: World models for model-based RL and planning usually need task-specific training on lots of interaction data. A pretrained tabular model that predicts in context could avoid that training, but its limits were unknown.

The authors frame next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs and test a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) on synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks. They compare against LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch, other regressors fitted on the same data, and models trained on the full dataset, for one-step and multi-step autoregressive prediction.

With limited transitions, TabFM beats LSTM and MLP models in almost all settings and is the most accurate regressor on locomotion, though a Gaussian process wins on smooth low-dimensional systems, and full-data models remain much better on most systems. Multi-step rollouts collapse to a trivial baseline with short context but improve a lot with long context, beating a trained LSTM on one task. Takeaway: tabular FMs are a good data-scarce predictor when you can give them long context, not yet a drop-in planner. Caveat: inference is about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM.

papers.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.tldr: Adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to estimate the nuisance functions in causal mediation analysis and adds a learned error head to build calibrated confidence intervals. Coverage is closer to nominal than comparators, and it runs 59.1 times faster than the bootstrap.
summary: Causal mediation analysis splits a treatment effect into indirect and direct paths and depends on several fitted nuisance functions. Tabular foundation models can estimate these in context, but valid confidence intervals must account for the uncertainty from fitting and combining them.

MediPFN uses a pretrained tabular foundation model for nuisance prediction and combines outputs with a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects, followed by supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization and independent calibration. The authors prove coverage bounds under standard assumptions.

Across experiments MediPFN reaches coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators and runs 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons. Takeaway: tabular FMs can serve as plug-in nuisance estimators for causal inference if you add an explicit calibration step, rather than trusting their raw predictions for intervals. Caveat: the abstract does not name the datasets or how close coverage gets, and evidence leans on simulated tables.
